1.

The present claim arises out of a detailed accident report (DAR), filed by the police in terms of the provision of Motor Vehicle Act in which petitioner Sanjay Grewal (aged about 29 years) sustained injuries.
2.

Brief facts of the case are that on 12.08.2020, petitioner was travelling on his motorcycle bearing no. DL-5SCC-9085 from his residence to his workplace at Sanjay Grewal (Dar) vs Ramkesh (377/20, Bp) on 7 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/89060048/
1 Chittranjan Park.

At 08.50 am, when he reached near Government School, Taj Pur Pahari, Badarpur, a Splendor motorcycle bearing no. DL-1SX-9398 (hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle) came driven in a rash and negligent manner and hit the motorcycle of the petitioner.
Due to the impact, petitioner fell and sustained injuries on his left leg and all over his body.
He was rushed to JPN Apex Trauma Center where he was treated.
3. An FIR no. 377/2020 dated 17.08.2020 u/s 279/337 IPC was registered against the driver of the offending vehicle.
After investigation, chargesheet was filed before concerned criminal court against the driver of the offending vehicle while present DAR was filed before this Tribunal.
4. Respondent no.1 is driver, Respondent no.2 is owner and Respondent no.3 is the insurance company of the offending vehicle.
5. In response to the DAR, Respondent no.1 and 2 filed their reply denying the allegations of rash and negligent driving by Respondent no. 1.
It is pleaded that the accident occurred solely CHARU GUPTA

sentences.text:
At 08.50 AM,
when he reached Government School, Tajpur Pahari, Badarpur, all of a sudden, a Splendor motorcycle bearing no. DL1-SX-9398, which was being driven by respondent Ramkesh, came in a very rash and negligent manner and hit the motorcycle of PW-1.
Due to the fall, PW-1 sustained grievous injuries in his left leg and injuries all over his body.
He was immediately taken to JPN Apex Trauma Center, AIIMS where the doctors declared injuries in his left leg to be grievous.
He stated that he was treated by private doctors at Delhi for about three months.
He deposed that he was 29 years of age at the time of accident and was working as a Telecaller with M/s Unique Enterprises.
He was getting a salary of Rs. 17,000/- per month but was unable to perform his duty for one year.

He deposed that he had spent more than Rs. 1,00,000/-
on his treatment/ special diet, convenience and other expenses.
He claimed Rs. 10,00,000/- as compensation for injuries, loss of income, loss of future income, loss of enjoyment, medical expenses, attending charges, pain and mental agony.

He relied upon his Aadhaar Card as Ex. PW1/1, Educational Proof as Ex. PW1/2, Disability Certificate as Ex. PW-1/3, MLC as Ex. PW1/4, Discharge Summary & OPC Cards as Ex. PW1/5,
Original medical bills as Ex. PW1/6 & DAR as Ex. PW1/7.

He was duly cross-examined by Ld.
Counsels for respondents.
Thereafter, petitioner evidence was closed.
Respondents did not lead any evidence.
8. Final arguments in details were addressed on behalf of the claimant/injured and the insurance company.

Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law,
proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit Sanjay Grewal (Dar) vs Ramkesh (377/20, Bp) on 7 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/89060048/
3 and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable.

Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & Ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken.
10. Before the standard of proof of negligence can be applied or discussed, the proof of negligence remains the lynch pin to recover compensation.

sentences.text: Without establishing or proving negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle, a claim to compensation cannot lie.
Hon'ble Supreme Court in Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Meena Variyal, AIR 2007 SC1069 observed:-

sentences.text: "...It may be true that the Motor Vehicle Act, insofar as it relate to claims for compensation arising out of accidents, is a beneficent piece of legislation.

It may also be true that subject to the roles made in that Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:

sentences.text: That does not mean that a Tribunal approached with a claim for compensation under the Act should ignore all basic principles of law in determining the claim for compensation.
Ordinarily, a contract of insurance is a contract of indemnity.

When a car belonging to an owner is insured with the insurance company and it is being driven by a driver employed by the insured, when it meets with an accident, the primary liability under law for payment of compensation is that of the driver.
Once the driver is liable, the owner of the vehicle becomes vicariously liable for payment of compensation.

It is this vicarious liability of the owner that is indemnified by the insurance company...".
11.
In the instant case, petitioner/injured Sanjay Grewal examined himself to allege that the offending vehicle was rash and negligent.
Despite disputing negligence, of the driver of the offending vehicle, he did not describe or elaborate in what manner the offending vehicle was being driver rashly or negligently.
It is only during cross-examination of PW-1 that it emerged that it is the petitioner himself who suddenly entered the road from a wrong side to avoid traffic congestion on his side of the road.
He has categorically admitted that he was riding a motorcycle bearing no. DL-5SCC-9085 on the wrong side and that he did not held any driving license at that time.
He also conceded that as he was driving without a license, a kalandara was filed against him by the police under Section 3/181/184 of MV Act.
He also admitted that no statement of any eyewitness was recorded.
Even the site plan and the FIR (that was lodged after almost 07 days from the accident) Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA

sentences.text: The fact that he did not hold a driving license further raises a presumption as to his negligence.

There is nothing on record to show in what manner respondent no. 1 was rash or negligent when it is an admitted fact that only to avoid traffic congestion on the side of the road that petitioner was travelling, he transgressed onto the wrong side.

The act of the petitioner cannot be ignored or underscored as mere traffic violation but is seen as an act endangering the life and safety of all others who were driving on their designated side of the road and following the traffic rules.
The fact that even a complaint was lodged with a police by the petitioner after conveniently waiting for 07 days, with no reasonable explanation for the delay, raises probability of after thought.

This is particularly so when the petitioner was discharged from the hospital on the same day and the injury suffered was not grave enough to have prevented the petitioner from reporting the matter to the police even by a 100 number call.
Furthermore, it is an admitted fact that the petitioner received Rs. 1 Lac as settlement amount from respondent no. 1.
In these circumstances, petitioner cannot be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong or derive unlawful enrichment from the Insurance Company for his own fault.

Though, the burden to prove the averments in the claim rests upon the petitioners and such burden is very less but it is not as if the mere averments of the claimant have to be believed without any evidence especially where the driver, owner and insurance Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA SANJAY GREWAL (DAR) Vs.
RAMKESH P.No. 7 Of 8GUPTA Date:
 MACT NO. 155/21 2025.08.08  04:23:26  +0530 company oppugn the same.

sentences.text:
In the present case, apart from bald averments and a delayed FIR, there is nothing to prove the rash or negligent driving by Respondent No. 1.
12.

Having regard to the material on record, circumstances and the above discussions, it is held that the petitioner had failed to prove negligence or any rash conduct on the part of the respondent no. 1.
Issue no. 1 is accordingly decided against the petitioner.
Issue no. 2
Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom?

OPP.

5 13.
For the reasons discussed in issue no. 1, petitioner is held not entitled to any compensation.
Issue No. 2 is accordingly decided against the petitioner.
In view of the above observations, present claim stands dismissed.
